ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A $5 \times 5$ square is covered with $1 \times 1$ tiles. The design on each tile is made up of three dark triangles and one light triangle (see diagram). The triangles of neighbouring tiles always have the same colour where they join along an edge. The border of the large square is made of dark and light triangles. What is the smallest number of dark triangles that could be amongst them?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, each 1×1 square tile is divided by two diagonals into 4 triangles along the edges. The square tile shown in the figure has 3 dark triangles and 1 light triangle, so each tile is equivalent to choosing exactly one edge among the upper, lower, left, and right four edges as the edge where the light triangle is located, and the remaining three edges are dark. Reasoning: Regard the 25 tiles of the 5×5 as 25 grid points. If two adjacent tiles share one edge, then the problem condition requires the colors of the triangles on the two sides of this edge to be the same. So if an internal common edge is light, it must simultaneously be the unique light edge of each of the two adjacent tiles; if it is not light, then both sides are dark. Thus the problem can be modeled as a matching problem: each cell must choose exactly one edge to be light; if an internal edge is chosen, then two adjacent cells are matched; if an outer boundary edge is chosen, then it contributes one light boundary triangle to the boundary. The boundary of the large square has a total of 20 boundary triangles. To make the number of dark boundary triangles smallest, the number of light boundary triangles must be made largest. Consider the 9 non-boundary cells in the central 3×3. They also must each have a unique light edge. If these central cells are matched with one another only inside the central 3×3, then each light internal edge covers two central cells. But 9 is odd, so it is impossible for all of them to be paired within the central 3×3; at least one central cell must be matched through a light edge to some boundary cell in the outer ring. For this outer-ring cell matched to a central cell, its unique light edge has already been used on an internal common edge, so it can no longer contribute a light boundary triangle. There are 16 boundary cells in the outer ring, and each can contribute at most 1 light boundary triangle, so the number of light boundary triangles is at most 15. Therefore the number of dark boundary triangles is at least 20−15=5. This lower bound can be attained: for example, let the upper-left cell of the central 3×3 be matched with the boundary cell directly above it; divide the remaining 8 central cells into 4 pairs of adjacent cells to be matched; and let each of the remaining 15 boundary cells choose an outer boundary edge as its light edge. In this way there are exactly 15 light triangles on the boundary, so there are exactly 5 dark boundary triangles.

method.method_draft: Model the tiling as a matching problem. From the diagram, read that each unit tile is divided into four edge-triangles by an X, with exactly one light triangle touching one side of the square and the other three side-triangles dark. Therefore each cell of the 5 by 5 grid must choose exactly one of its four sides to be light. The text condition that neighbouring tiles have the same colour where they join means that if a shared side is light, it is the unique light side for both adjacent cells; otherwise it is dark for both. Treat each tile as a vertex. A chosen light shared side matches two adjacent vertices; a chosen light border side matches one boundary vertex to the outside. To minimize dark border triangles, maximize chosen light border sides. There are 20 border triangles total. The 9 non-border cells in the central 3 by 3 block must all be covered by light sides; light sides entirely within the 3 by 3 block cover them in pairs, so because 9 is odd, at least one central cell must be matched to an outer-ring cell. That outer-ring cell cannot also have a light border triangle. Since there are 16 outer-ring cells and each can contribute at most one light border triangle, at most 15 border triangles can be light. Hence at least 20 - 15 = 5 border triangles are dark. Then show achievability by giving a matching: match the upper-left cell of the central 3 by 3 block to the boundary cell directly above it, pair the other 8 central cells in four adjacent pairs, and let each of the remaining 15 boundary cells choose one exterior side as its light side. This gives exactly 15 light border triangles, so the minimum dark border count is 5.

图像描述：图中每个 1×1 方砖被两条对角线分成 4 个沿边的三角形。图示的方砖有 3 个深色三角形和 1 个浅色三角形，因此每块砖等价于在上、下、左、右四条边中恰好选择一条边作为浅色三角形所在边，其余三条边为深色。

推理：把 5×5 的 25 块砖看作 25 个格点。若两块相邻砖共用一条边，则题设要求这条边两边的三角形颜色相同。所以一条内部公共边若为浅色，就必须同时是相邻两块砖各自唯一的浅色边；若不是浅色，则两边都是深色。

于是问题可建模为匹配问题：每个格子必须恰好选择一条边为浅色；若选择内部边，就匹配两个相邻格子；若选择外边界边，就给边界贡献一个浅色边界三角形。

大正方形边界共有 20 个边界三角形。要使深色边界三角形最少，就要使浅色边界三角形最多。

考虑中央 3×3 的 9 个非边界格子。它们也都必须有唯一一条浅色边。如果这些中央格子只在中央 3×3 内部互相匹配，则每条浅色内部边覆盖两个中央格子。但 9 是奇数，因此不可能全部在中央 3×3 内部两两配对，至少有一个中央格子必须通过浅色边匹配到外圈的某个边界格子。

这个被中央格子匹配到的外圈格子，其唯一浅色边已经用在内部公共边上，所以它不能再贡献浅色边界三角形。外圈共有 16 个边界格子，每个最多贡献 1 个浅色边界三角形，因此浅色边界三角形最多为 15 个。

所以深色边界三角形至少为 20−15=5 个。

这个下界可以达到：例如让中央 3×3 左上角格子与其正上方的边界格子匹配；其余 8 个中央格子分成 4 对相邻格子匹配；剩下 15 个边界格子各选择一条外边界边作为浅色边。这样边界上正好有 15 个浅色三角形，因此深色边界三角形正好有 5 个。

method.method_draft: Use a contradiction focused on the central 3 by 3 block. From the diagram, each border tile can have at most one light triangle on the outside border, because each tile has only one light triangle total. The large 5 by 5 square has 16 boundary tiles and 20 outside border triangles. Suppose fewer than 5 border triangles were dark. Then more than 15, hence at least 16, border triangles would be light. Since only the 16 boundary tiles can contribute border light triangles and each contributes at most one, every boundary tile would have to place its unique light triangle on the outside border. Therefore every edge between the outer ring and the central 3 by 3 block would be dark. But then each of the 9 central tiles would still need its one light triangle, and it could only be on an edge shared with another central tile. Such light shared edges pair central tiles two at a time, impossible for 9 tiles. Thus at least 5 border triangles must be dark. For equality, arrange the central 3 by 3 block so that one central edge cell has its light side shared with a neighbouring outer-ring tile, pair the remaining 8 central cells internally, and put the light triangle of every other outer-ring tile on the outside border. Then exactly 15 outside border triangles are light and 5 are dark.
method.CoT_raw:
图像描述：附图中的小正方形瓷砖被两条对角线分成四个三角形区域。每块砖有三个深色三角形和一个浅色三角形；这个唯一的浅色三角形位于某一条边对应的三角形位置上，其余三条边对应深色三角形。因此，在拼成大正方形时，每块砖等价于“选择至多一条边为浅色”，实际上正好有一条边对应浅色三角形。

推理：5×5 大正方形共有 25 块砖，其中外圈边界砖有 16 块，中间 3×3 区域有 9 块。大正方形外边界由 20 个单位边组成，所以外边界上共有 20 个边界三角形。每块边界砖总共只有一个浅色三角形，因此每块边界砖至多能在外边界贡献 1 个浅色三角形。

用反证法证明至少有 5 个深色边界三角形。假设外边界深色三角形少于 5 个，则外边界浅色三角形多于 15 个，也就是至少 16 个。由于只有 16 块边界砖能贡献外边界浅色三角形，并且每块至多贡献 1 个，所以每一块边界砖都必须把自己的唯一浅色三角形放在外边界上。

这样一来，外圈砖朝向中间 3×3 区域的边都必须是深色。相邻砖在公共边上的颜色必须相同，所以中间 3×3 区域中每块砖朝外圈的边也都是深色。于是中间 9 块砖各自的唯一浅色三角形只能放在中间 3×3 区域内部的公共边上。

但是一个内部浅色公共边会同时满足相邻两块中心砖的唯一浅色三角形要求，也就是把中心砖两两配对。中间共有 9 块砖，是奇数，无法全部两两配对。因此假设矛盾，外边界至少有 5 个深色三角形。

下面说明 5 可以达到。选择中间 3×3 区域边上的一块中心砖，让它的浅色边与相邻外圈砖共享；剩下的 8 块中心砖可以在 3×3 去掉这块边上中心砖后两两沿内部公共边配对。外圈中除这块特殊外圈砖外，其余 15 块边界砖都把唯一浅色三角形放在外边界上；特殊外圈砖把浅色边朝向刚才那块中心砖。这样外边界恰有 15 个浅色三角形。由于外边界总共有 20 个三角形，所以深色三角形数为 20−15=5。故最小值是 5。

raw_record.original_question: A $5 \times 5$ square is covered with $1 \times 1$ tiles. The design on each tile is made up of three dark triangles and one light triangle (see diagram). The triangles of neighbouring tiles always have the same colour where they join along an edge. The border of the large square is made of dark and light triangles. What is the smallest number of dark triangles that could be amongst them?
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: In the figure, each 1×1 square tile is divided by two diagonals into 4 triangles along the edges. The square tile shown in the figure has 3 dark triangles and 1 light triangle, so each tile is equivalent to choosing exactly one edge among the upper, lower, left, and right four edges as the edge where the light triangle is located, and the remaining three edges are dark.

Reasoning: Regard the 25 tiles of the 5×5 as 25 grid points. If two adjacent tiles share one edge, then the problem condition requires the colors of the triangles on the two sides of this edge to be the same. So if an internal common edge is light, it must simultaneously be the unique light edge of each of the two adjacent tiles; if it is not light, then both sides are dark.

Thus the problem can be modeled as a matching problem: each cell must choose exactly one edge to be light; if an internal edge is chosen, then two adjacent cells are matched; if an outer boundary edge is chosen, then it contributes one light boundary triangle to the boundary.

The boundary of the large square has a total of 20 boundary triangles. To make the number of dark boundary triangles smallest, the number of light boundary triangles must be made largest.

Consider the 9 non-boundary cells in the central 3×3. They also must each have a unique light edge. If these central cells are matched with one another only inside the central 3×3, then each light internal edge covers two central cells. But 9 is odd, so it is impossible for all of them to be paired within the central 3×3; at least one central cell must be matched through a light edge to some boundary cell in the outer ring.

For this outer-ring cell matched to a central cell, its unique light edge has already been used on an internal common edge, so it can no longer contribute a light boundary triangle. There are 16 boundary cells in the outer ring, and each can contribute at most 1 light boundary triangle, so the number of light boundary triangles is at most 15.

Therefore the number of dark boundary triangles is at least 20−15=5.

This lower bound can be attained: for example, let the upper-left cell of the central 3×3 be matched with the boundary cell directly above it; divide the remaining 8 central cells into 4 pairs of adjacent cells to be matched; and let each of the remaining 15 boundary cells choose an outer boundary edge as its light edge. In this way there are exactly 15 light triangles on the boundary, so there are exactly 5 dark boundary triangles.
